title: South Africa’s benchmark transition carries over R98 trillion of Jibar derivatives and a clearing-date problem
summary: Deputy Governor Rashad Cassim’s 3 November remarks at the Market Practitioners Group conference put a scale on South Africa’s benchmark transition. By September, global ZARONIA-related derivative exposures exceeded R18.5 trillion, while global Jibar derivative exposures still exceeded R98 trillion. The figures describe exposures linked to benchmarks. They are neither trading turnover nor losses at risk. The speech credits LCH SwapClear for offshore exposure data. Both figures are reported as lower bounds, so they do not establish an exact market share. They nevertheless show why the timing of contract conversion matters alongside the integrity of the successor fixing. Cassim traced the reform to 2018 and to a problem with reference rates built from quotations supplied by a small set of banks. An overnight rate drawn from actual wholesale deposit transactions addresses the quality of the benchmark even though rewriting contracts that name the old rate remains a separate undertaking.

Cassim distinguished clients who renegotiate, positions that can switch automatically under existing arrangements, and difficult legacy contracts that cannot be amended in time. Proposed amendments to the Financial Sector Regulation Act would allow replacement benchmarks to be designated. Parliamentary passage and presidential assent were still pending. Large clearing houses also needed to schedule conversion of outstanding derivatives. If a cleared hedge switches on one date and an underlying loan or bilateral contract switches on another, both parties can remain exposed to the difference between benchmarks even when the original positions were well matched. The potential consequences include valuation, hedging and operational risk. That mismatch helps explain the authorities’ decision to move final Jibar publication from December 2026 to May 2027. Cassim judged the extra five months unlikely to create major new transition costs. He considered the greater risk to be ending publication before the legal mechanism and clearing timetable were ready.

Cassim described ZARONIA as a near-risk-free rate based on substantial overnight wholesale deposit transactions, with a small and stable spread to the policy rate. Contracts written on that benchmark could express views on monetary policy more directly. He cited overnight index swaps and Treasury floating-rate notes as examples. A new observation on the successor curve might nonetheless reflect a different liquidity premium, instrument mix or clearing convention from the old Jibar point. Preserving overlap observations, conventions and exposure data would make a historical policy transmission study more reliable than simply joining the two curves at cessation.

The remarks also distinguished benchmark transition from a separate discussion about loan pricing. The Prime Lending Rate stood at a fixed 350-basis-point spread over the SARB rate, while banks set individual loans at negotiated spreads to Prime. Cassim cited an estimated R4.7 trillion of domestic Prime-linked exposures and argued that removing the intermediate reference could make loan pricing easier to understand. He referred to a consultation and stressed the need for care with implementation dates. Moving a contract to a different base rate can be economically neutral if the contractual spread changes correspondingly. The speech did not announce a 350-basis-point reduction in borrowing costs or a date for discontinuing Prime.

Finally, Cassim identified two markets in which the authorities wanted more activity. A liquid government bond market coexisted with limited private-sector issuance, and reduced government issuance might create more room for private fundraising. In repo, the domestic concern was insufficient activity and obstacles to mobilising collateral. The SARB and market participants were studying plumbing and regulatory constraints. These observations point to potential research on funding and liquidity after transition. They do not supply changes in issuance, spreads, leverage or realised borrowing costs attributable to the speech.

questions.question: Where would a mismatch between clearing-house and cash-product conversion create the greatest basis exposure?
questions.detail: Identify outstanding hedges and their underlying cash flows by remaining maturity, reset dates, compounding conventions and legal conversion triggers. Compare cleared and bilateral schedules and estimate exposures only on the overlapping cash flows that would reference different rates. Global gross exposures establish scale, but netting and offsetting positions matter for the value actually at risk across counterparties.

questions.question: Does the ZARONIA curve transmit monetary surprises differently as its liquidity grows?
questions.detail: Compare changes in overnight-index swaps and equivalent-maturity Jibar instruments around timestamped policy announcements during their overlap. Use executable prices, bid–ask spreads and available volume separately from outstanding exposure, and check whether any divergence reflects credit or liquidity compensation. That would test Cassim’s claim about expressing policy views more directly without assuming a near-risk-free benchmark removes every source of market noise.

questions.question: Would replacing Prime simplify borrower comparisons while preserving existing contractual economics?
questions.detail: Follow proposed conventions through actual loan templates and repricing schedules, recording the policy base, negotiated spread, fees and reset frequency. Compare equivalent borrowers and products before and after an implemented change. The fixed 350-basis-point reference margin and R4.7 trillion estimate indicate its relevance, but neither number identifies the borrower-specific spread or predicts an actual change in a household’s interest payment.

limitation: The amounts are benchmark-linked derivative exposures. The speech provides no conversion-by-conversion valuation effects or estimates of gains and losses.
